pins.name: SR-20 Wine Spires pullout / Burgundy Col climbers' trail
SR-20 Wine Spires pullout / Burgundy Col climbers' trail

text: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR 20) to the unmarked pullout on the south side of the highway near milepost 166, about 0.7 mile west of the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff (east of Washington Pass and its hairpin). No pass is needed to park at this roadside pullout.

pins.name: SR-20 Wine Spires / Silver Star pullout (~MP 166, ~4 mi east of Washington Pass)
Wine Spires / Silver Star Trailhead (SR-20 MP 166)
Wine Spires / Silver Star Trailhead (SR-20 MP 166)

text: From Washington Pass, drive SR-20 east about 3.75 miles, past the hairpin turn, to the next long pullout on the east shoulder near milepost 166, opposite Silver Star. The climbers' path is not signed — it drops off the east side of the embankment.

Park at the pullout on SR-20 near milepost 166, about three and three-quarters miles east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain. There's no numbered Forest Service trail here — this pullout is simply the start of an established but unofficial boot path used by climbers heading for Burgundy Col.

Downclimb or rappel a short way onto the Silver Star Glacier and descend it west and northwest to Burgundy Col, roped for crevasses. Cross the col and follow the Burgundy Col climbers' trail down to Highway 20 near milepost 166, about 4 miles east of Washington Pass, where a shuttle car saves the long road back to Cedar Creek.

Turn off SR-20 onto Forest Road 400 about 4 miles east of Washington Pass and follow it roughly a mile to the Cutthroat Lake Trailhead, at about 4,500 ft. Park there and start at the trailhead kiosk on the maintained Cutthroat Creek Trail #483. Don't confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which leaves an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass and has no maintained

Turn off Hwy 20 about 4.4 to 4.5 miles east of Washington Pass onto Forest Road 400, signed for the Cutthroat Lake/Creek Trail, and drive roughly a mile to the trailhead lot. The lot sits at about 4,500 ft and has restrooms. Don't confuse this with the Cutthroat Peak approach, which starts from an unmarked highway pullout about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass with no maintained trail.

From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 18 miles and turn south onto Forest Road 5310-200 between mileposts 176 and 175, about half a mile east of the Klipchuck Campground turn. Follow it to its end at a gravel pit and park; the trail starts at the pit's southeast corner. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

From Winthrop, drive about 17 miles west on SR 20 (or about 115 miles east from Burlington) and turn south on FR 200, signed for Cedar Creek. Drive 0.8 mile to the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issued wilderness permit is available at the trailhead.

Drive SR-20 to the signed Easy Pass turnoff between mileposts 151 and 152 and follow the short spur to the small lot. Camping beyond the pass is inside the national park, so the backcountry permit has to be in hand before you start — there is no self-issue option at the trailhead.

From Marblemount, drive SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) east about 45 miles and turn right between mileposts 151 and 152 onto the short spur signed for Easy Pass, ending at a lot for about 10 cars. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required (self-issue at the kiosk). The highway closes in winter, so the trailhead is reachable only once it opens for the season.

Drive Highway 20, the North Cascades Highway, to the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, at about 3,700 feet. Highway 20 is a seasonal route, typically open from mid-April through mid-November and closed the rest of the year, so check conditions before you go.

Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the small pullout where the highway crosses Silver Star Creek, about 8.5 miles east of Washington Pass near milepost 171, at roughly 3,450 ft. The highway over the pass closes in winter.

Bacon Creek Road leaves WA-20 near milepost 112 and runs up to a road-end parking spot at about 850 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A 2018 rockslide near mile 4.7 limits the road to high-clearance vehicles beyond that point, and the drivable end shifts year to year with washouts, so a bad year simply adds road-walking to the front of the approach. Nothing is signed or maintained fr

Drive Lost River Road out of Mazama, then Harts Pass Road 5400 past Ballard and River Bend campgrounds, staying left to the rough road end at about 2,700 ft. There is a signboard, vault toilet and stock ramp here. The Monument Creek and Robinson Creek trails leave from the same stretch of road, so check the sign before starting.

From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 11 miles and turn left onto Thornton Lakes Road between mileposts 117 and 118, just west of Newhalem. Follow this rough gravel road about 5 miles to the trailhead at road's end, around 2,500 ft; high clearance is recommended.

From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 11 miles and turn left onto Thornton Lakes Road between mileposts 117 and 118. Follow this rough gravel road about 5 miles to its end at about 2,500 ft; a high-clearance vehicle is recommended. Overnight stays in the park need a backcountry permit.

From SR 20 about 14 miles west of Winthrop, turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140) and follow it through Mazama to the end of the pavement at about 7.5 miles, where it becomes Harts Pass Road (FS 5400). In about a quarter mile turn right into the Monument Creek Trailhead at about 2,400 ft. No parking pass is needed; self-issue a free wilderness permit at the kiosk.

From SR 20 at the Mazama turnoff (about 14 miles west of Winthrop), turn onto Lost River Road and after half a mile turn left to stay on it. Follow it about 7.5 miles to the end of the pavement, then 1.25 miles on gravel FR 5400 to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right, at about 2,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park; fill out the free self-issue wilderness per

From Winthrop, drive Highway 20 west about 15 miles and turn right onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140). After half a mile turn left to stay on Lost River Road, drive 7.5 paved miles, then continue about 1.25 miles on gravel Forest Road 5400 to the Robinson Creek Trailhead on the right, at about 2,500 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park.

From SR-20 near milepost 82, turn north on Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive about 14 mi to the Baker Dam turnoff. Cross the dam on FS Road 1106, turn left on FS Road 1107 and follow it 8 to 9 mi to a signed spur on the left, which ends at the Anderson and Watson Lakes Trailhead in about 1 mi. The road is long and rough; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

From SR 9 north of Sedro-Woolley, turn right onto Mosquito Lake Road just after crossing the South Fork Nooksack and drive about 9 miles. Just past the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, turn right onto FR 38 and drive about 11 miles to the Elbow Lake Trailhead on the right, with parking across the road. pins.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)

text: Drive SR 20 about 60 miles - roughly an hour and a half - east from Burlington and park at the Goodell Creek Campground turnout at milepost 119, just west of Newhalem. The highway is paved all the way to here, and the trailhead sits west of both of SR 20's winter closure gates (Ross Dam at milepost 134, and Newhalem at milepost 120 in harder winters), so driving access to this trailhead does not d

pins.name: Goodell Creek Trail Trailhead (climbers' access near Upper Group Campground)

text: Park at the Goodell Creek Group Campground on SR-20 near Newhalem, at about 600 feet. The climbers' path begins behind a large boulder at the back of the Upper Group Campground. If you'll be camping in Terror Basin, North Cascades National Park requires a backcountry camping permit — pick it up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (walk-up only, no advance reservations for th

pins.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground
Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground
Thunder Creek Trailhead (Colonial Creek Campground, South Loop)

text: The trailhead is at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, just past milepost 130 — turn into the campground and find the trail starting at the amphitheater in the south loop, at about 1,200 feet. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, is required for the overnight bivy at the Borealis Glacier.

pins.name: Gorge Creek bridge / Gorge Creek Falls parking, SR 20 (~MP 123)

text: Drive SR 20 to the bridge over Gorge Creek, about 2.6 miles east of Newhalem and about the same distance west of the Gorge Lake causeway and the Diablo turnoff. Watch the sharp curve at the east end of the bridge. Park in the lot at the west end; the east lot is signed for motorhomes and oversize vehicles. There is no trail: the route leaves the highway directly.

From Winthrop, take the East Chewuch River Road north about 6.5 miles and, before it crosses the Chewuch River, turn right onto FR 37. Follow FR 37 about 13 miles, turn left onto FR 39 and drive about 7.5 miles, past Freezeout Pass, to Tiffany Springs Campground at about 6,760 ft. FR 37 from Conconully reaches the same junction. The gravel is rough, closed to trailers and usually snowbound until l

Reach the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of Forest Service Road 13, via the Baker Lake Highway and the Sulfur Creek Road turnoff. Park at the trailhead lot; a recreation pass is required and is not sold on site, so buy it ahead or pay by phone. No wilderness permit is needed.

From WA-20 at milepost 82, turn north onto Baker Lake Road (FS Road 11) and drive 12.5 miles to just past the Rocky Creek bridge. Turn left on FS Road 12 for 3.6 miles, then stay right on FS Road 13 for 5.3 miles to its end at the Schriebers Meadow (Park Butte) trailhead, about 3,360 ft. Road 13 is potholed and rocky; high clearance helps. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

From Sedro-Woolley, drive SR 20 east 16 miles to milepost 82 and turn left (north) on Baker Lake Road (FS 11). After 12 miles turn left on FS 12 and drive 3.6 miles to the FS 13 junction; stay right on FS 13 (Sulphur Creek Road) for 5.3 miles to its end at the Park Butte / Schriebers Meadow trailhead, about 3,360 ft. pins.name: Panther Creek / East Bank Trailhead (SR 20, milepost 138)

text: Drive SR 20 to milepost 138 and park at the East Bank Trailhead, at about 1,800 ft. From the lot the trail drops briefly to the bridge over Ruby Creek, so there is no further driving once you are here. If you come before the highway opens for the season, the gate is back at milepost 134, and parties have biked the roughly four miles in to the trailhead from there and continued on foot or ski.

The trailhead is a small pullout on SR-20 about 6.4 miles east of Newhalem near milepost 127, with room for roughly six cars. Park on the highway side and cross the road on foot to reach the signed trail. No parking pass is needed, but an NPS backcountry permit from Marblemount is needed to camp; SR-20 is closed through the winter and normally reopens in April or May, which sets the earliest possi

The Pyramid Lake Trailhead is a signed gravel pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, about 21 miles east of Marblemount and 6.4 miles past Newhalem, just past the Diablo turnoff at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft. The maintained Pyramid Lake Trail starts across the highway from the pullout. Day hiking needs no permit, but an overnight camp in the park does: pick up the NPS wilderness permi

pins.name: Stetattle Creek Trailhead, Diablo (approach; closed for post-fire hazards, check status)

text: Drive SR 20 to milepost 126 and turn into the town of Diablo (not Diablo Dam). The trailhead is just past the Stetattle Creek bridge at the entrance to town; park in the small turnout on the right, leaving room for others. Overnight stays need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east about 20 miles to milepost 126 and turn left at the sign for Diablo. Cross the Stetattle Creek bridge, bear right, and park beside the river across from the domed swimming pool; the Sourdough Mountain Trail starts behind the pool building at about 900 ft. Overnight stays in North Cascades National Park need a backcountry permit.

pins.name: Harts Pass Trailhead (Pacific Crest Trail north)

text: From SR 20 at the Mazama turnoff (about 14 miles west of Winthrop), go through Mazama and follow Lost River Road about 7 miles to the end of the pavement, then continue on Harts Pass Road (FR 5400), a narrow, steep, single-lane gravel road with pullouts, about 12 more miles to Harts Pass at about 6,200 ft. Trailers are prohibited. Park where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north. A free self-issue P

FS-5400 runs about 20 miles of narrow gravel from Mazama up to the pass, with steep drop-offs and no guardrail, and it stays snowed in well into early summer. At roughly 6,200 ft this is the highest drivable pass in Washington, so the trip opens as a rolling high traverse rather than a climb.
From SR 20 at Marblemount, drive east about 28 miles, past Newhalem and Diablo Lake, to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking near milepost 134.

pins.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20) — via Ross Lake water taxi/hike to Big Beaver, then off-trail to Access Creek/Luna Camp

text: The trailhead is a pullout on SR-20 near milepost 134. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required before you start.

From SR 20 at the Mazama junction, cross into Mazama and turn left on Lost River Road (County Road 9140), which becomes Harts Pass Road, FR 5400, where the pavement ends. Follow this narrow road (no trailers) roughly 19 miles to Harts Pass. At the guard station turn right on the Slate Peak road, FR 5400-600, and park at its second switchback below the gated road end, near 6,900 ft. A free self-iss

FS-5400 runs about 20 miles of narrow gravel from Mazama up to Harts Pass, and the Slate Peak spur climbs on to the trailhead at Slate Pass, roughly 6,900 ft, below the gate under Slate Peak that ends the highest drivable road in Washington. It usually opens in early July once the snow clears, and parking at the top is limited.
